ubo_and_aml_profiling.statutory_law_governance: Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009 (AML/CFT Act), Companies Act 1993 (as amended by the Companies (Beneficial Ownership) Amendment Act 2023), and the Financial Markets Authority (FMA) regulations. The Companies Office maintains a beneficial ownership register accessible to government agencies, law enforcement, and tax authorities under strict confidentiality protocols.

ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory screening against the New Zealand Sanctions List (Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade), the United Nations Security Council Consolidated List, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List, the European Union Consolidated Financial Sanctions List, and the UK HM Treasury Consolidated List. Additionally, all directors, shareholders, and beneficial owners must undergo Politically Exposed Persons (PEP) screening using commercial databases (e.g., Dow Jones, World-Check) and enhanced due diligence for any PEP or high-risk jurisdiction. Ongoing transaction monitoring and periodic re-screening are required under the AML/CFT Act 2009, with a risk-based approach for low-risk micro-SaaS entities.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: New Zealand Companies Office - Name Reservation Portal (https://www.companiesoffice.govt.nz)
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Company names must be in English or Māori, using the Latin alphabet. Non-English characters must be transliterated into English phonetically. The name must not be misleading, offensive, or imply a connection with the Crown or government. Four-tier naming conventions: (1) the name must end with 'Limited' or 'Ltd' (unless exempt), (2) must not be identical or too similar to an existing name, (3) must not contain restricted words without approval, and (4) must not be contrary to public interest.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Companies Act 1993 (New Zealand) — sections 12 to 18 (Incorporation), section 51 (Registered Office), sections 88-99 (Registers and Records), sections 151-156 (Director Qualification and Appointments), section 189 (Share Allotment), and Schedule 2 (Default Constitution)
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: New Zealand Companies Office, Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) — Companies Register (companies-register.companiesoffice.govt.nz)
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Application for Incorporation filed electronically under section 12 of the Companies Act 1993; issuance of a Certificate of Incorporation and automatic allocation of a New Zealand Business Number (NZBN)
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: None — New Zealand imposes no statutory minimum paid-up capital. A company may be incorporated with a single fully-paid ordinary share of nominal value NZ$1.00. No escrow deposit, capital commitment account, or bank verification account is required under the Companies Act 1993 (sections 12-15).
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en: RESOLUTION OF THE SUBSCRIBER BOARD OF DIRECTORS OF [COMPANY NAME] LIMITED (the 'Company'). Pursuant to the Companies Act 1993 and the Company's Constitution, the Subscriber Board resolves: 1. SHARE CAPITAL SUBSCRIPTION: The Company shall issue and allot [NUMBER] ordinary shares at NZ$1.00 par value each to the initial subscriber shareholder(s) named in the Application for Incorporation, fully paid, with no escrow deposit or capital verification account required under New Zealand law. 2. REGISTERED OFFICE ADOPTION: The registered office is fixed at [ADDRESS, NEW ZEALAND], and statutory registers and company records shall be maintained there or at another lawful location approved by the Board under section 51 of the Companies Act 1993. 3. OFFICER APPOINTMENTS: [NAME] is appointed Director and Company Secretary, and [NAME] is appointed Managing Director, effective immediately, each holding office until the close of the first Annual General Meeting or earlier vacation under sections 152-155. 4. GENERAL: The Directors and any one of them are authorised to complete all Companies Office filings, open corporate bank accounts, affix the common seal (if any), and retain professional accounting advisers as deemed necessary. RESOLVED AND CONFIRMED this [DATE].

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Company Name Search and Availability Clearance
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: New Zealand Companies Office — Name Reservation & Availability Tool (companies-register.companiesoffice.govt.nz)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Conduct a company name availability search on the public Companies Register. Verify that the proposed name is not identical or almost identical to an existing registered company or reserved name, is not likely to mislead, does not imply Crown or charitable status, and is not offensive within the meaning of sections 20-22 of the Companies Act 1993. If desired, formally reserve the proposed name for a non-renewable period of 20 working days at no charge prior to filing the incorporation application.
required_dossiers: Proposed company name in English (maximum 100 characters)
Name reservation request (optional, via online portal)
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the name is declined or queried by the Registrar, the applicant must respond in writing addressing the stated objections, or submit an alternative proposed name. An application for reconsideration may be made under section 22(2) of the Companies Act 1993.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Subscriber shareholder(s) and proposed directors, with external legal and accounting advisers as applicable
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Prepare and execute a written Company Constitution in English, or expressly adopt the default constitution in Schedule 2 of the Companies Act 1993. Obtain from each proposed director a signed Consent to Act as Director under section 152. Executed subscriber meeting minutes/resolution must fix the registered office address in New Zealand and set the initial share allotment parameters (share class, number, and consideration).
required_dossiers: Company Constitution (PDF) duly executed
Consent to Act as Director signed by each proposed director
Subscriber resolution/minutes on registered office and initial share allotment
Identity documentation (e.g., RealMe-authenticated identity verification) for each proposed director
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: Correct any constitutional inconsistency with the mandatory provisions of the Companies Act 1993 (e.g., director vacancy and indemnity rules under sections 155 and 162). Re-execute defective consent forms and resubmit the governance pack.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Lodgment of the Application for Incorporation
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: New Zealand Companies Office — Online Companies Register (companies-register.companiesoffice.govt.nz)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Log in with RealMe authentication and file the electronic Application for Incorporation. Enter the approved company name, the New Zealand registered office address, proposed officers and directors, shareholder and share structure, and the election regarding the Constitution. Attach the executed Constitution and the Consents to Act as Director in PDF format. Confirm all identity details match the consent forms exactly; notarization is not required for online lodgment under New Zealand practice.
required_dossiers: Completed online Application for Incorporation
Company Constitution (PDF)
Consent to Act as Director (PDF) for each proposed director
RealMe identity verification attestation and AML due diligence file
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Registrar issues a query or refuses registration, the applicant must provide precise clarifications and corrected particulars within 20 working days from the date of the query. A corrected application may be resubmitted without an additional fee where the deficiency arose from a registry error.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Payment of Official Registration Fee and Issuance of Certificate of Incorporation
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: New Zealand Companies Office (MBIE) — Payment Services and Company Register
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Settle the statutory registration fee of NZ$101.50 (approximately USD 63) by credit or debit card through the secure online payment portal. Upon payment settlement, the Registrar registers the company, issues the Certificate of Incorporation, and automatically allocates a New Zealand Business Number (NZBN) and company number. The incorporation date is the date stated on the certificate; the company comes into existence as a legal personality from that moment and the certificate must be preserved as conclusive evidence of incorporation.
required_dossiers: Accepted incorporation application reference number
Payment instrument and online payment receipt
Certificate of Incorporation (registry-issued PDF)
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If payment fails, the draft application is securely discarded without charge and a fresh application must be re-initiated. If the Certificate of Incorporation contains an error, file a written request for administrative correction under section 311 of the Companies Act 1993 and obtain an amended certificate.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: First Post-Incorporation Governance Board Meeting and Establishment of Statutory Registers
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Board of Directors of the incorporated company; company records maintained at the registered office
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Convene the first board meeting within seven days of incorporation (physically or by virtual meeting). Approve the issue and allotment of share certificates, record shareholders in the share register, adopt a contract execution policy authorizing Paddle and Lemon Squeezy merchant agreements, confirm the registered office location, appoint banking mandates, and record all resolutions in the minute book. Maintain the register of directors, register of shareholders, share transfer register, and records of directors' certificates in accordance with sections 88-99 of the Companies Act 1993.
required_dossiers: Signed share certificates for all issued shares
Register of shareholders and register of directors
Minutes of the first board meeting (governance records)
Executed board resolution delegating bank mandates and SaaS platform agreement authorities
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: Rectify any discrepancy in statutory records by way of a corrective board minute. File updated director or shareholder particulars with the Companies Office within 10 working days of any change to avoid pecuniary penalty exposure under section 126 of the Companies Act 1993.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Associated Administrative Registration — IRD Number and Tax Profile Onboarding
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Inland Revenue Department (IRD) New Zealand, using NZBN enterprise registration integration
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Use the company's NZBN and the Inland Revenue online enterprise registration service to obtain the company's IRD number. Assess the mandatory GST registration threshold (NZ$60,000 of New Zealand taxable supplies in a 12-month period); for the consumer micro-SaaS subscription model, evaluate voluntary GST registration and the zero-rating position applicable to exported digital services. If local employees are engaged, establish PAYE payroll registrations and obtain the employer tax file number.
required_dossiers: Certificate of Incorporation and NZBN allocation notice
Company resolution authorising the appointed fiscal agent or tax agent
Projected New Zealand turnover schedule for GST registration determination
Completed IRD online company registration application (IR342 or equivalent e-filing)
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the IRD queries the business classification or GST registration position, the company must submit a written description of the cloud software subscription services and underlying revenue model, and may engage a New Zealand tax agent to file objections or apply for an IRD binding ruling to cure the uncertainty.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.competent_industrial_authority: Not applicable — ISIC 6201 (Computer Programming, Consultancy and Related Activities) does not trigger industrial licensing in New Zealand; the CK_IC entity establishes no manufacturing, factory, or heavy industrial undertaking requiring accreditation from an industrial licensing board.
industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.operating_license_title: Not applicable — no occupational licence, manufacturing permit, or sector-specific trade certificate is statutorily required for a micro-SaaS subscription software business operating from registered office premises. Should the company later lease physical office space, Building Act 2004 compliance for the premises will apply to the landlord/occupier, but no business operating licence is imposed.

environmental_impact_assessment_eia.agency_name: Environmental Protection Authority (EPA) New Zealand — named for completeness; no consent pathway is triggered by this classification.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.classification_tier: Exempt — the activity does not constitute a 'proposal of national significance' and falls outside the EIA-required activity list under the Resource Management Act 1991 schedules. A pure software/cloud-service operation involves no land disturbance, no construction, and no discharge of contaminants. If physical hosting infrastructure is later contracted, the EIA obligations would rest with the data-centre facility operator.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.discharge_and_emissions_standards: Not applicable — the operation generates no wastewater effluent, no VOC combustion sources, and no hazardous waste streams. The National Environmental Standards for air quality and freshwater apply only if physical infrastructure is subsequently established. General e-waste disposal, if any, must comply with the Waste Minimisation Act 2008 and the Trans-Tasman Hazardous Waste Agreement once physical office equipment is decommissioned.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.civil_defense_and_occupational_clearance: No civil-defence clearance or occupational workplace licence is prescribed for remote cloud software operations. If a leased office is opened, the operator must obtain a Building Warrant of Fitness covering specified fire-safety and life-safety systems under the Building Act 2004, and must comply with the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015, including documented emergency planning. Service continuity planning aligned with the Civil Defence Emergency Management Act 2002 is additionally recommended to support micro-SaaS uptime commitments.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Inland Revenue Department (Inland Revenue; Te Tari Tāke), the national revenue authority of New Zealand, administered through the myIR secure online portal at www.ird.govt.nz. The New Zealand Customs Service (Tariff) separately governs export declarations and border clearance through the Trade Single Window.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: (1) If the International Company is incorporated in New Zealand, an IRD number issues automatically upon Companies Office incorporation via the integrated IRD-registration process. (2) For a non-resident or foreign-incorporated company, submit Form IR742 'Application by a non-resident company for an IRD number' to Inland Revenue, either directly or through an approved New Zealand tax agent, together with the certificate of incorporation, registered office and principal place-of-business details, constitutional documents, and director/shareholder particulars. (3) GST registration is effected on the same IRD number by lodging a GST101A application or registering through myIR once taxable turnover reaches NZD 60,000 in a 12-month period or, alternatively, through voluntary registration. (4) No separate VAT identification number exists; the IRD number serves as the single statutory tax identification number for both income tax and GST purposes. (5) Processing typically concludes within 5–10 business days for non-resident applications lodged by an NZ agent, subject to anti-money-laundering verification.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.default_entity_tax_classification: Entity_Level_Taxation — a New Zealand-incorporated International Company is ordinarily tax-resident in New Zealand and taxable at the entity level at the 28% corporate income tax rate on worldwide income. The tag 'Tax_Exempt_Zone' referenced in the entity structure metadata is not a statutory New Zealand tax category; New Zealand has no general offshore tax-exempt zone, and any such characterisation would be recharacterised under the general anti-avoidance rules in Part GA of the Income Tax Act 2007 and the associated tax-avoidance jurisprudence.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: Look-Through Company (LTC) election under Subpart HB of the Income Tax Act 2007: a closely held New Zealand company may elect full fiscal transparency, causing profits and losses to be attributed to shareholders and removing entity-level income tax; New Zealand has no US-style 'check-the-box' election, but the LTC election is the functional New Zealand equivalent. Hybrid and branch mismatch rules in Part FM of the Income Tax Act 2007 statutorily neutralise or deactivate elections that would otherwise create double non-taxation. Qualifying Company (QC) elections have been closed to new companies since 31 March 2011.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: New Zealand GST — Goods and Services Tax imposed under the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985 (an invoice-credit value-added tax)
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: NZD 60,000 — mandatory registration is triggered where the taxable supply of goods and services in New Zealand exceeds NZD 60,000 in a 12-month period (s 51 GSTA 1985); voluntary registration is permitted below the threshold, including for non-resident remote-services suppliers.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: No real-time fiscal clearance, continuous transaction control, digital stamping, or government API clearance is imposed on New Zealand GST. Invoicing is governed by tax invoice rules (ss 24–24D GSTA 1985), and e-invoicing is voluntary under the Peppol interoperability framework adopted by Inland Revenue's e-Invoicing network. GST returns (GST101) are filed digitally through myIR on a six-monthly, two-monthly, or monthly cycle (monthly filing is mandatory where taxable turnover exceeds NZD 24 million per annum), with payment of GST due by the 28th day following the end of each taxable period.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Exported tangible goods are zero-rated where the supplier proves the goods were exported from New Zealand within 28 days of the time of supply (s 11(1)(a)/(ca) GSTA 1985). For the SaaS service line, zero-rating applies to (i) B2B 'remote services' supplied to a non-resident recipient who receives the services outside New Zealand under an enforceable contract with the supplier and is not in New Zealand at the time of supply (s 11A(1)(k)–(l)); and (ii) B2C 'remote services' supplied over the internet or an electronic network to non-resident individuals who are outside New Zealand when the supply takes place (s 11A(1)(m)). The supply is zero-rated only where the supplier holds sufficient commercial and documentary evidence that the recipient's jurisdiction and location are foreign; supplies to New Zealand-resident consumers remain standard-rated, triggering mandatory non-resident GST registration if New Zealand consumer turnover exceeds NZD 60,000 per annum.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: New Zealand Customs export declaration (lodged through the Customs Trade Single Window; outward entry with HS classification and quantity)
Bill of Lading or Air Waybill (the carrier-issued transport document evidencing physical export from New Zealand)
Tax invoice (or credit note) issued under ss 24/24G GSTA 1985 explicitly identifying the zero-rated supply and the zero-rating basis
Foreign currency sales contract, subscription, or order documentation identifying the non-resident counterparty or consumer
Inward Remittance Certificate or SWIFT MT103 bank proof evidencing external payment of the NZD or foreign-currency export consideration
Shipment or parcel carrier tracking and outward manifest match report evidencing cross-border transit
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: Inland Revenue's GST export-audit programme scrutinises zero-rating claims for corroborative shipping and residency evidence; failure to substantiate triggers GST reassessment under s 78 GSTA 1985 (retrospective clawback plus use-of-money interest), shortfall penalties under the Tax Administration Act 1994 of 20% (failure to take reasonable care), 40% (unacceptable tax position), 100% (abusive tax position), or 150% (evasion), and criminal liability under s 143A for knowingly providing false GST returns, with fines up to NZD 50,000. Anti-fraud clawback extends to any refunds granted where the underlying export proceeds, including the 180-day repatriation evidence, are later reversed, repatriated onshore, or applied to New Zealand-resident consumption.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Te Pūtea Matua) — the national central bank exercising statutory oversight under the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act 1989, the Non-bank Deposit Takers Act 2013, and the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009 (AML/CFT Act), with delegated prudential supervision over registered banks, licensed insurers and non-bank lending institutions in New Zealand.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: New Zealand maintains full convertibility on both current and capital account transactions, having accepted Article VIII obligations of the International Monetary Fund's Articles of Agreement. There are no exchange control laws, no prior central bank approval requirements, no capital repatriation restrictions, and no limitation on holding foreign currency accounts domestically or offshore. The New Zealand dollar (NZD) is a freely floating fiat currency with no official band. For the contracting International Company (IC) structured as a Tax-Exempt Zone entity with a Cook Islands legal origin and a New Zealand operational nexus, profit remittance to non-resident shareholders encounters zero statutory foreign-exchange hurdles, and the sole residual constraints arise from taxation rules (i.e., non-resident withholding tax on interest/dividends paid to foreign corporate shareholders, typically reduced to 0% under domestic law or an applicable double tax agreement where the recipient is a company) and bank-level documentary due diligence. The IC is generally outside the New Zealand tax net where central management and control are exercised offshore; nonetheless, capital subscription and revenue repatriation can be routed through New Zealand clearing systems without any prior Reserve Bank approval.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: New Zealand imposes no export proceeds surrender obligations, no mandatory conversion ratios, and no statutory repatriation timelines. A New Zealand-resident or New Zealand-operating exporter, including the IC, may lawfully retain export receipts in foreign currency, maintain offshore collection accounts, delay conversion, or repatriate funds at the commercial discretion of the board. The only reporting touchpoints are (i) AML/CFT transaction monitoring by the receiving bank for cash transactions at or above NZD 10,000 and for wire transfers above NZD 1,000, and (ii) statistical data collection by the Reserve Bank of New Zealand for balance of payments reporting, neither of which requires any conversion or surrender of proceeds.

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.account_class: Capital Escrow Account (NZD) + Operational Multi-Currency Account

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Feasibility Rating: Medium-High. Global fintech EMIs and payment platforms (Wise, Airwallex, Payoneer, and the Merchant-of-Record rails Paddle and Lemon Squeezy expressly listed as target payment rails) are lawfully available to the IC for collection and payout purposes, subject to the bank-grade look-through AML/KYC policies of the underlying tier-1 acquiring banks. Legal constraints: (i) most digital EMIs decline tax-exempt offshore structures lacking demonstrable substance; (ii) the Cook Islands incorporation flag requires the EMI to verify the ultimate beneficial ownership and source of funds at the same standard as a regulated bank; (iii) NZD and AUD collection efficiency requires a local New Zealand settlement account, which EMIs may or may not provision; and (iv) where the EMI is not a New Zealand registered financial institution, the IC may be required by the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 and the AML/CFT Act to appoint a local agent for service of process. The recommended architecture is a primary NZ bank account used for treasury concentration and a secondary EMI used for low-value, high-volume consumer SaaS collections to minimize FX conversion charges.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: For a non-resident International Company, the rule at the four major New Zealand registered banks (ANZ, BNZ, ASB, Westpac) is a mandatory physical appearance of at least one director and the ultimate beneficial owner at account opening, or a live video appointment accepted only on a discretionary, case-by-case basis under the electronic identity verification standards of the Identity Verification Code of Practice 2013. In practice, remote onboarding is achievable where the IC engages (i) a licensed New Zealand corporate service provider or law firm acting as an introducer under the AML/CFT due diligence provisions, (ii) a private banking relationship with an existing face-to-face link, or (iii) an approved digital identity verification provider matching the bank's electronic KYC framework. The Cook Islands IC structure will normally trigger additional authentication steps, including a notarized board resolution, apostilled incorporation instruments, and at least one in-person interview with the bank's compliance officer in Auckland, Wellington, or Christchurch, unless the introducing firm carries a formal compliance undertaking. Kiwibank generally declines non-resident ICs absent a substantive New Zealand residency nexus.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Tax-exempt offshore International Company with zero or opaque local substance
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Certificate of Incorporation and Certificate of Good Standing issued by the Cook Islands Financial Services Development Authority; certified register of directors, register of charges and register of members; ultimate beneficial ownership declaration and corporate structure diagram; board resolution authorizing account opening and designating signatories; New Zealand virtual office or service address agreement; service contracts of New Zealand-based directors or consultants; customer subscription agreements and Paddle/Lemon Squeezy merchant agreements evidencing genuine commercial activity; latest audited or management accounts.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Source of funds and source of wealth for the initial shareholder capital injection
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Personal bank statements, investment portfolio statements and income tax returns of the ultimate beneficial owner; executed share subscription agreement; SWIFT MT103 record of the remittance showing the exact capital path; forward-looking financial model of the micro-SaaS; historical payout statements from Paddle or Lemon Squeezy demonstrating low-ticket recurring consumer transactions; a source-of-wealth declaration sworn by the shareholder before a notary public.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Jurisdiction risk red flag triggered by the Cook Islands / offshore tax-haven classification
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Compliance certificate from the licensed Cook Islands registered agent confirming the IC is in good standing under the International Companies Act 1980-81; economic substance documentation, if applicable, under the Cook Islands International Companies (Economic Substance) Regulations; legal opinion confirming the IC is not tax resident in New Zealand under the tie-breaker rules of the New Zealand-Cook Islands Double Tax Agreement and is not tax resident in the Cook Islands; FATF/OECD member status evidence for New Zealand and the Cook Islands competent authority statement; board minutes and resolutions demonstrating real decision-making in a physical jurisdiction.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Suspicious payment pattern inconsistent with a genuine operational SaaS company
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Signed commercial contracts with customers, cloud hosting providers (AWS/Azure), and independent contractors; recurring monthly statements from the Merchant-of-Record platform; payroll or contractor remittance evidence; SaaS operational metrics (monthly recurring revenue, subscriber counts, refund policy); an accounting trail reconciling the Merchant-of-Record payouts to the bank account; and a written treasury narrative describing expected transaction velocity and counterparty locations.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Beneficial ownership opacity arising from a trust, nominee, or layered corporate structure
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Complete trust deed and any amendments, if the IC is owned by a trust; certified trust register; statutory declaration from the trustee identifying all settlors, protectors and discretionary beneficiaries; nominee declaration and acknowledgements of bare nominee capacity; passport copies of all directors and ultimate beneficial owners; AML/CFT-compliant ultimate beneficial owner diagram; PEP and sanctions screening results showing clear status.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: The compliant path for an inbound equity or shareholder loan injection into the IC's New Zealand account is as follows: (i) the board passes a resolution approving the share subscription or shareholder loan, the account opening, and the signatory mandate; (ii) the remitting party sends a SWIFT MT103 with the narrative field stating 'Shareholder equity injection - subscription of Class A ordinary shares in [IC Name]' or 'Shareholder loan disbursement under facility agreement dated [date]'; (iii) the NZ receiving bank will not require a statutory purpose code but will internally classify the transaction as a capital account inflow for its regulatory reporting, and will screen the remitter and the underlying narrative against sanctions and PEP databases; (iv) the bank will verify the transaction against the account's declared purpose and may request the signed share certificates, updated register of members, and the source-of-funds documentation if the amount exceeds NZD 50,000 or is unusual for the account profile; (v) no Reserve Bank of New Zealand approval is required, and the funds become fully available for treasury use once the bank's internal post-transaction monitoring is satisfied. For an injected amount above NZD 250,000, a formal board minute and bank's Large Transaction Review form should be executed to preclude inadvertent structuring red flags.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: The operative clearing rails for the consumer micro-SaaS's outbound disbursements are: (i) SWIFT MT103 for all international transfers, including supplier payments to cloud hosting providers, software license fees to subcontractors, legal and accounting fees to New Zealand advisory firms, and periodic profit distributions to the non-resident shareholder; (ii) the New Zealand BECS (Bulk Electronic Clearing System) and the Reserve Bank's ESAS (Exchange Settlement Account System) real-time gross settlement rail for same-day NZD payments to domestic counterparties; (iii) SEPA (Single Euro Payments Area) for euro-denominated vendor payments from the bank's EUR sub-account, and the ACH/Fedwire networks for USD-denominated clearing; (iv) Commercial Letters of Credit are not a standard resource for SaaS royalty or subscription flows but remain a permissible and enforceable rail where an enterprise procurement contract expressly demands one — the IC may open a standby or documentary LC through its New Zealand bank for low-ticket sums backed by uncommitted facilities; and (v) the Merchant-of-Record platforms Paddle and Lemon Squeezy will settle net subscription revenue to the IC's designated NZD or USD account via SWIFT or local clearing, eliminating the need for the IC to maintain separate merchant acquiring accounts. To accelerate recurring disbursement release, the IC should pre-register all beneficiary accounts in the bank's dashboard and provide the bank with a standing instruction template containing the approved legal basis for each recurring payment.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Plain-vanilla FX spot transactions — executed on request with no underlying documentation requirement at existing bank dealing desks (ANZ, BNZ, Westpac) for converting USD, EUR, AUD or GBP collections into NZD at market rate plus a standard corporate margin of 0.3% to 0.9%.

Deliverable FX forward contracts (standard tenors of 1 week to 12 months) — permitted under the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 for corporate end-users; execution requires a signed treasury dealing agreement and demonstrable underlying exposure, e.g., a rolling 12-month USD revenue forecast from Paddle/Lemon Squeezy payouts.

Non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) for settlement in restricted or less-liquid Asian currencies (e.g., CNY, PHP, IDR, VND) where the IC collects consumer SaaS receivables from those jurisdictions; NDFs are accepted by New Zealand banks as standard OTC hedging instruments and require no ISDA agreement for tenors under 12 months.

Cross-currency swaps (dual-currency liability management) — permitted for any asset-backed or term-lending structure above NZD 1 million; execution requires an ISDA master agreement, a board resolution, and the bank's credit committee approval.

OTC FX option contracts (plain-vanilla European puts and calls) — available on an application-only basis; banks generally allow these only in combination with a forward or collar to evidence commercial hedging purpose, and frequency limits are imposed to prevent classification as speculative dealing under the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013.

FX collar/zero-cost structures — permitted for the micro-SaaS scale where the board adopts a formal hedging policy (e.g., hedge ratio of 30% to 70% of forecast net exposed cash flows for a 6-to-12 month horizon) to evidence the commercial purpose exemption from the financial adviser licensing regime.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual Government Fee (Company Renewal) for the International Company, remitted by the licensed registered agent to preserve the company's legal existence and good standing.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Registrar of International Companies, Cook Islands Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC).
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Payable annually in advance in the month of the anniversary of the certificate of incorporation; the registered agent must remit the fee on or before the anniversary date to maintain continuous good standing, with no statutory grace period.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late payment attracts penalties prescribed in the FSC fee regulations, typically 10% of the annual fee (US$50), and may incur further administrative charges; continuing non-payment after formal statutory notice exposes the company to administrative strike-off under the International Companies Act 1981–82 (as amended), resulting in deregistration and dissolution, with the company's assets vesting in the Crown as bona vacantia.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual Beneficial Ownership and Register Confirmation Certificate (directors' declaration to the registered agent confirming the accuracy of the register of members, register of directors, and UBO records).
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Licensed registered agent (FSC-licensed corporate services provider) acting under the Cook Islands AML/CFT compliance framework; not filed with the FSC.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Annually in conjunction with the government-fee renewal, and immediately upon any share transfer, allotment, or change of directors or beneficial ownership.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Non-delivery of the confirmation entitles the registered agent to refuse the annual renewal or terminate agency services; sustained non-compliance may cause the agent to resign, and the company must then appoint a replacement licensed agent within the statutory period or face deregistration for failure to maintain a registered agent.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: None. Cook Islands International Companies are unconditionally exempt from statutory audit and from preparation, submission, or publication of financial statements to the FSC, regardless of turnover, total assets, number of shareholders, or public-offering status.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: No statutory accounting framework applies to an International Company. Voluntary financial statements, if prepared for management or parent-group consolidation, may be presented under IFRS, US GAAP, or the accounting standards of the jurisdiction of effective management (e.g., New Zealand XRB-Accredited IFRS if the decision-making parent is NZ-based).

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: The Cook Islands maintains no public UBO register and imposes no annual UBO filing to the FSC. Under the AML/CFT regime, the licensed registered agent must obtain, verify, and hold current beneficial ownership and control documentation. The company's directors must deliver, at each annual renewal and upon every share transfer, a written confirmation that the register of members, register of directors, and UBO file are accurate; agents typically perform an internal register audit by comparing the confirmation against the statutory registers and CDD records. All registers and UBO information remain confidential and are not open to public inspection or filed with the government registry.

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.registered_office_or_agent_market_range_: US$1,200 – US$3,500 per annum (typical market range for a licensed Cook Islands registered agent providing registered office, company secretary, registered agent services, and AML/CFT compliance support for a micro-SaaS International Company).
recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: Not statutorily required; a voluntary independent audit or agreed-upon-procedures review, if requested by a SaaS payment processor or investor, typically ranges from US$4,000 to US$10,000 per engagement.

corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: Standard New Zealand corporate tax rate of 28% applies to any entity that is a New Zealand tax resident or that derives New Zealand-sourced income. For the International Company (IC) operating a consumer micro-SaaS business, taxable income will typically be limited to New Zealand-sourced royalties or business profits derived through a fixed establishment. Statutory tax holidays are not available under the general Income Tax Act 2007. Preferential deductions include R&D tax credits of 15% on eligible R&D expenditure (for entities with tax-loss or where R&D undertaking conditions are met) and the 20% R&D intensity tax credit where R&D intensity exceeds 5%; however, these are available only to New Zealand-resident entities carrying on business in New Zealand. A non-resident IC with no New Zealand fixed establishment and only passive cross-border SaaS subscription revenue from New Zealand customers will normally have nil New Zealand corporate income tax, as SaaS subscription payments are characterized as business profits rather than royalties, absent a New Zealand fixed establishment or a royalty-bearing contract for the use of copyrighted software.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: NZ-IR4 (Income Tax Return for Companies) filed via Inland Revenue's myIR portal or approved tax software gateway (e-File / EDI)
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: Standard balance date: 31 March. The IR4 return is generally due and tax payable by 7 July following the balance date. For a non-standard balance date approved by Inland Revenue, the due date is seven months after the balance date. Provisional tax is required if residual income tax exceeds NZD 5,000, with instalments typically on 7 May, 7 September, and 15 January for standard balance-date taxpayers. For a non-resident IC deriving only final withholding-tax income (interest or royalties subject to NRWT), no IR4 is required; the payer deducts non-resident withholding tax at source.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Net taxable income or loss after applying income tax act deduction rules
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident IC with no New Zealand-sourced income enters nil. If the IC has New Zealand-sourced royalties, include the gross royalty amount adjusted for any allowable expenses only if a New Zealand fixed establishment exists; otherwise the income is subject to final NRWT and not reported on IR4.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Box 2 / Losses carried forward or offsets
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Tax losses brought forward from prior years and group loss offsets claimed
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A non-resident IC cannot carry forward New Zealand tax losses unless it has a New Zealand fixed establishment and is assessable in New Zealand. For a New Zealand-resident IC, losses carry forward up to 5 years and are subject to continuity of ownership (49% continuity rule) or business continuation tests.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Box 3 / Imputation credit account and credits
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Imputation credits, R&D tax credits, foreign tax credits, and other offsets used to reduce residual income tax
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident IC may claim foreign tax credits for NRWT or foreign taxes paid on income included in the New Zealand return, attaching Form IR8 with the return. If the IC is non-resident with no New Zealand tax return filing obligation, no credit claim is made; instead final NRWT is the ultimate tax.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: The amount of income tax remaining after all credits and offsets, which triggers provisional tax obligations
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: For non-resident IC that is nevertheless required to file IR4 due to a fixed establishment or inventoried New Zealand-sourced income, the residual tax is the excess of calculated tax over NRWT credits attached to the income.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Box 5 / Resident withholding tax (RWT) on interest and dividends
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: RWT deducted from New Zealand-source interest and dividends derived during the year
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident IC normally derives interest and dividends subject to NRWT rather than RWT. Where the IC holds shares in a New Zealand company, fully imputed dividends are generally exempt from further income tax in New Zealand; the company payer deducts NRWT at 30% or the reduced rate under a DTA.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing penalties for IR4: an initial NZD 250 penalty for failure to file, plus a further NZD 250 penalty if not filed within 60 days of the initial notice, and an additional NZD 500 penalty where the failure continues after 6 months. Late payment penalties: 1% of the unpaid amount for each day of default, capped at 10% of the tax assessed; an additional late payment penalty of 10% of the unpaid tax is imposed if the tax remains unpaid after 12 months. Use-of-money interest under sections 120K–120M of the Tax Administration Act 1994 accrues on unpaid tax at approximately 10.44% per annum. Failure to file IR67 (non-resident withholding tax return) for a pay-as-you-earn style obligation attracts a late filing penalty of NZD 250 plus a further NZD 50 per 28 days of non-compliance. Criminal penalties for knowingly providing false returns: fines up to NZD 50,000 for a company and imprisonment for up to 5 years for individuals under section 143A.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: The statutory New Zealand non-resident withholding tax (NRWT) rate on dividends paid to a non-resident company is 30%. This rate is reduced to 15% for fully imputed dividends paid to a non-resident company that holds 10% or more of the voting power in the dividend-paying company. New Zealand's dividend withholding tax regime also imposes a supplementary dividend election in limited cross-border investment arrangements; the standard DTA rates for portfolio dividends are typically 15%, and for substantial shareholdings (at least 10%), 5% or 15% depending on the treaty. The International Company (CK_IC) is presumed to be non-resident unless central management and control is in New Zealand; if non-resident, dividends from New Zealand payers are subject to NRWT at the applicable treaty rate, subject to entitlement.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: To apply for DTA relief reducing NRWT on dividends, interest, or royalties, the non-resident recipient must complete the relevant Inland Revenue declaration form (IR67S for non-resident withholding tax declaration) and provide a valid tax residence certificate (TRC) issued by the competent authority of the jurisdiction in which the IC is tax resident. The IC must sign a declaration that it is the beneficial owner of the income and that no arrangement has the purpose of obtaining treaty benefits (a purpose or limitation-of-benefits test applies under New Zealand's DTAs and relevant anti-abuse rules). The New Zealand payer must obtain the declaration and TRC before the payment is made or before the return is filed to apply the reduced rate at source; if the treaty relief is claimed after the fact, the non-resident must apply for a refund from Inland Revenue within the statutory four-year assessment period, attaching the IR67S, TRC, and evidence of beneficial ownership. Inland Revenue may require additional proof of economic substance or genuine business activity under the General Anti-Avoidance Rule (section BG 1) if the arrangement is considered treaty shopping.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Statutory NRWT rates in New Zealand for non-residents are 15% on interest and 15% on royalties paid to non-resident recipients, unless the payer elects to pay the approved issuer levy (2%) on certain registered interest-bearing securities. Under New Zealand's DTA network, the most common reduced rates are: interest 10% for most treaty partners (e.g., Australia, UK, US, Japan), but 15% in certain cases; royalties generally 5% or 15% depending on the treaty and the nature of the copyrighted work, with an option for 10% under some modernised treaties. For a consumer micro-SaaS business, payments received by the IC from New Zealand consumers for cloud-based software subscriptions are not 'royalties' under New Zealand domestic law or most DTAs because the SaaS contract is not a transfer of copyright; rather the revenue is business profits. Consequently, no NRWT is payable on SaaS subscription fees if the IC has no fixed establishment in New Zealand. If the IC licenses downloadable software to users, the characterization may shift to royalties, triggering NRWT at 15% (or treaty-reduced rate). Interest paid to the IC by a New Zealand debtor would trigger NRWT at 15% or treaty rate.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: The relevant threshold for mandatory New Zealand transfer pricing documentation: a taxpayer must prepare and retain contemporaneous transfer pricing documentation if the taxpayer has international related-party transactions exceeding NZD 10 million in aggregate in an income year, or if related-party transactions in a common asset-intangible or financial category exceed NZD 10 million. For a micro-SaaS IC with annual global revenue below NZD 50 million and cross-border related-party transactions below NZD 10 million, no master file or local file is statutorily mandatory; however, if the IC has any cross-border related-party dealings exceeding NZD 4 million in aggregate, Inland Revenue may request documentation and the taxpayer must substantiate arm's length outcomes based on the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines. The lacking contemporaneous documentation triggers reversals of burden of proof in tax disputes and potential documentation penalties. New Zealand does not prescribe a formal master file / local file regime under domestic law; compliance follows the OECD TP Guidance as applied through sections GC 1–GC 14 of the Income Tax Act 2007. For an IC deriving SaaS subscription income through a New Zealand resident related-party distributor or a platform, transfer pricing must be evidenced by a written intercompany agreement and comparable benchmarking, particularly where Capex and premium intangible returns are shared.
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: New Zealand does not have a codified Economic Substance Regulation (ESR) in the same form as the UAE or BVI; however, statutory economic substance principles arise under: (i) the General Anti-Avoidance Rule (section BG 1, Income Tax Act 2007), (ii) the reconstruction powers under sections GB 1 and GC 1–GC 4i, and (iii) the tax residence tests under sections YD 2 and YD 5A, which deem a company resident in New Zealand if it is incorporated in New Zealand or if its central management and control is exercised in New Zealand, even if not incorporated in New Zealand. For a CK_IC International Company structured as a tax-exempt offshore vehicle, if it has no office, employees, decision-making substance, or independent administration in its own jurisdiction and its directors act from New Zealand, it will be treated as a New Zealand tax resident, causing worldwide income taxation at 28%. The economic substance doctrine requires that the IC's revenue, bank accounts, board decisions, and corporate records genuinely demonstrate that it is not a sham; otherwise Inland Revenue may recharacterise the arrangement and assess the New Zealand resident developer as the true taxpayer. The Interest Limitation Rule and the non-resident financial arrangement rules similarly deny deductions for interest paid to a related non-resident that lacks substance on excessive debt-funded acquisition structures. As the entity is a Low_Risk_Standard consumer micro-SaaS, the practical requirement is that the IC must maintain real economic substance in compliance with the underlying Cook Islands IC regime, including a registered agent, registered office, licensed trustee (if in a trust), and financial accounts, to avoid being classified as a shell or transparent vehicle.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Deliberately failing to disclose New Zealand-sourced income or capital gains from the SaaS subscription business, submitting false IR4 returns, using offshore accounts to hide consumer revenue, destroying accounting records, or knowingly mischaracterising royalty income as business profits to avoid withholding tax obligations.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Under section 143A of the Tax Administration Act 1994, an individual convicted of tax evasion is liable to imprisonment for up to 5 years and a fine up to NZD 50,000 (or twice the amount of tax evaded, whichever is greater). A company can be fined up to NZD 50,000 per offence; the court may order the payment of evaded tax plus interest and shortfall penalties. Civil shortfall penalties under section 141D: 100% of the shortfall for evasion, 50% for abusive tax position, 40% for a significant position without adequate disclosure, and 20% for an unacceptable tax position. Inland Revenue may raise amended assessments within the extended period (unlimited where evasion or fraud), seize assets, issue a bankruptcy notice, and prosecute through the Commissioner's criminal investigation unit. The Financial Transactions Reporting Act and the computer misuse legislation also apply if records are altered or deleted.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who aid, abet, direct, or connive in tax evasion are jointly and severally liable under section 140 of the Tax Administration Act 1994. Personal civil liabilities include the unpaid tax, shortfall penalties, and interest. Criminal prosecution of a director can result in imprisonment up to 5 years and personal fines of up to NZD 50,000; if the director is also a shadow director controlling the IC, the court may treat the IC as the director's alter ego and pierce the corporate veil. Directors may face travel restrictions through arrest warrants issued in criminal proceedings, and courts may impose restraining orders freezing personal assets and bank accounts under the Criminal Proceeds (Recovery) Act 2009.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Operating the International Company as a hollow shell with no employees, no physical presence, no director meetings, no minutes, no proper accounting records, no bank account substance, and no actual commercial decision-making where the ultimate beneficial owner (UBO) carries on the SaaS business from New Zealand using New Zealand-resident contractors and New Zealand payment infrastructure.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Inland Revenue can apply the GAAR and reconstruction provisions to recharacterise the arrangement, deem the IC to be a New Zealand tax resident (central management and control test), and assess the entire worldwide income of the IC to New Zealand tax at 28%. Penalties under section 141A–141D for a tax avoidance arrangement: 50% of the shortfall for an abusive tax position, plus use-of-money interest. Additionally, failure to maintain proper accounting records is an offence under section 50 of the Tax Administration Act 1994 and the Financial Reporting Act 2013, attracting fines up to NZD 10,000 and potentially director liability. Under the Companies Act 1993, a shell company that fails to meet its obligations may be struck off the register, and any person knowingly concerned in the operation of the company for a fraudulent purpose can be personally liable for the debts of the company under section 320. The statutory anti-money laundering regime requires verification of UBO and source of funds, and a shell profile will be reported as suspicious to the New Zealand Financial Intelligence Unit.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who cause the IC to trade without a legitimate business purpose are liable for reckless trading under section 135 of the Companies Act 1993. The court may order the director to personally contribute to the company's assets for creditor losses, and in tax cases the corporate veil is pierced under the common law 'façade' principle where the company is used to evade existing obligations. Directors can be disqualified from managing companies for up to 5 years under the Companies Act 1993 for repeated offending, and in serious cases imprisonment up to 5 years under the Crimes Act 1961 for fraud offences. A director who signs tax returns while the entity is a sham may be personally liable for the tax shortfall under the strict liability offence in section 143B, with fines up to NZD 25,000 and, for persistent non-payment, imprisonment.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: AML / Money Laundering Through Payment Processors
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Using the micro-SaaS payment rails (Paddle, Lemon Squeezy) to process consumer payments for the benefit of undisclosed beneficial owners, deliberately splitting revenue across multiple bank accounts in different jurisdictions to avoid banking thresholds, converting SaaS subscription revenue into cryptocurrency without KYC verification, or structuring transactions to evade reporting obligations to New Zealand's Financial Intelligence Unit under the AML/CFT Act.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Under the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009, reporting entities that fail to conduct customer due diligence, report suspicious transactions, or implement risk-based compliance programmes are subject to civil penalties of up to NZD 200,000 for an individual and up to NZD 2 million for a body corporate. Criminal penalties for laundering the proceeds of crime under the Crimes Act 1961 and the Criminal Proceeds (Recovery) Act 2009 carry imprisonment for up to 7 years and fines up to $300,000. The court may order forfeiture of all property that is the proceeds of a serious crime. Additionally, merchant of record or payment processor contracts (Paddle, Lemon Squeezy) may be terminated for cause upon suspicion of AML breaches, causing immediate account closure, holdback of funds for 180 days, and contractual liability.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and senior managers of a reporting entity can be individually prosecuted for consenting to or knowingly being a party to money laundering under section 245 of the Crimes Act 1961; penalties include imprisonment for up to 7 years and large fines. Under the AML/CFT Act, the Financial Markets Authority can ban a person from being a senior manager or director of any financial institution for life in egregious cases. Where a director uses the IC as a vehicle to launder funds, the court may issue a pecuniary penalty order and restraint order over the director's personal property; directors face civil liability for the amount laundered through their bank accounts, and travel bans may be imposed as part of bail conditions in criminal proceedings.
